h: Signatures, scenes in the garden and the rest of the family homes
p: Look carefully at the windows as you go round. Over the years, visitors scratched their names into the glass of one window, and among the signatures are some famous ones, including Sir Walter Scott. It is a quirky reminder that people have been making the pilgrimage here for over two hundred years.

The garden is a treat too. It is planted with flowers and herbs mentioned in Shakespeare's works, and on many days actors perform short scenes or speeches out in the garden. You might catch a bit of Hamlet or Romeo and Juliet between rooms, which is a brilliant way to hook kids who think Shakespeare is all dusty books.

Allow around an hour to an hour and a half for the Birthplace itself. If you want more, the Trust's other houses tell later parts of the story: Anne Hathaway's Cottage in Shottery, where his wife grew up; Mary Arden's Farm at Wilmcote, the home of his mother; and Shakespeare's New Place, the site of his family home in later life. Hall's Croft, the home of his daughter Susanna and her husband, is also in town.

Then finish at Holy Trinity Church by the river, where Shakespeare is buried. The riverside walk from the town centre past the Royal Shakespeare Theatre is a lovely way to get there, especially on a sunny evening when the swans are out and the boats are bobbing on the Avon.
Tip: the town centre gets very busy in summer and at weekends, so an earlier start gives you a calmer wander round the rooms.
